utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, it was announced that you would have a preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and good morning. One of our witnesses missed his flight. Actually, he didn't miss it; the aeroplane didn't take off, so there was no flight from Sarajevo yesterday. And it might be that tomorrow, after we finish the next witness, we will not be able to have another one, because that gentleman is supposed to come tonight at some late night hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how it develops and how to adapt our schedule to that situation. The witness can be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time with the following: On the 2nd of July the Defence has requested that it be permitted to make submissions in writing with regard to the tendering of associated exhibits for witness Vladimir Radojcic. The Chamber understands through an informal communication that the Prosecution has followed up with the Defence in this regard and has also asked the Chamber to set a deadline for the Defence to make the aforementioned submissions. The Chamber wonders whether the Defence today would be in a position to give an update to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we should be able to get that on file, I would think, by Thursday of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not today? Today is impossible? Or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Today is impossible because of the other work we have, Your Honours, and the fact that I have one of the witnesses that I have to meet with tomorrow. I can try but I cannot guarantee that it would be completed by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thursday is okay, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination with a few questions. Could I ask you not so speak too quickly and to focus your answers very much on the questions that are put to you rather than to elaborate in areas which were not part of the question. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another topic. During the NATO bombings of 1995 and when the UN Rapid Reaction Forces fired upon the VRS, what actions did you take in relation to UNPROFOR and other UN personnel on your territory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were forcers on our territory, including military observers. At the check-points where these forces were, the UNPROFOR units, they moved out of there, they withdrew and left towards the Muslim side. As we were attacked, and the UNPROFOR forces had openly sided with the enemy, we - and I can't recall right now - we declared five to seven military observers prisoners of war, and detained them in the house of Savo Golubovic, who was a forestry engineer and the manager of forestry in Trnovo. I would like to stress that we did not mistreat them. Every officer was allowed to call their command and their family, to provide them with their address. We brought a doctor, and whoever needed medical assistance, we offered it. We provided them with food that we also used. So they had three meals a day. And there were no -- we did not use any kind of force against them, nor were any restraints used. We abided by the Geneva Conventions in terms of the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The UNMO that were detained, were they disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We disarmed them. We took their rifles. We left their side arms. We left the pistols that they had on them and even the ammunition for it. And the guards that guarded them were the organs of my military police and I can say that they treated them very fairly. And as for the leader of this group, who was supposed to contact the brigade command in case of need, I decided that that would be the most senior officer among the guards. He was a major. And I can also say that I also established -- we established direct telephone lines between him and the brigade command centre so that in the event that this officer had a need, he could always contact the brigade command so that the information would reach me as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever receive any orders from a superior command requesting you or demanding that you tie these UNMO personnel to military installations and use them as human shields?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order that I received from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps said that everything that was in my defence zone should be captured and that they should be treated, that they should have the status of prisoners of war. I never received any orders that they could be restrained or they should be tied to some facilities or any of the military targets - warehouses, military depots or so on. I only saw this on TV and I can only assume that this must have been the work of some paramilitary forces or some renegade members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not interested from your assumptions on what may have happened, what you saw on television. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and good morning. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You'll find him to your right. And Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I note in your statement that has been offered into evidence now that you were in Brcko in August of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the chief of the military department of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the JNA, the TO and work organisations, for all the structures of the then-All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you held that position until when?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in that position until an order arrived from the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of July -- I apologise, August or July, 1992, that all military departments should be disbanded or shut down, and that military departments shall be established at the level of the municipality, the National Defence, and this would then be the department that we would deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were in Brcko for quite a while. I take it you were very familiar with the events on the ground during that period, August 1991 through July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the military department is concerned, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also had a position of Chief of Staff of the Brcko Brigade, did you not? I think you mentioned something about that in your statement to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew, I believe this was two days later, the 21st of May 1992, I received oral orders from the commander of the military district that I should, in addition to my regular duties, become the Chief of Staff of the brigade in Brcko and this -- I was actually working temporarily in this position and this began --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the dates when he assumed his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date that you assumed that duty?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from the 20th -- 23rd of May 1992 up until the 15th August 1992, where I stood in for the Chief of Staff of the 1st Posavina Brigade in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was known informally as the Brcko Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what people called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was the brigade that was part of the VRS from May, June, July, onward in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your rank when you were still with the JNA as the chief of the military department?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had been a major for the fourth year already, and I came from another post where I was a deputy commander of the border battalion in August, in mid-August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So aside from knowing the events that occurred on the ground in the Brcko area during this period of the spring of 1992, you must have been very familiar with the geographic area around Brcko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may just clarify something, the military department or the draft board of Brcko was only --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a very simple --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is also very simple, Mr. Prosecutor, because the zone of the military board did not correspond to the Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a very simple question. Were you familiar with the geographic area around Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with the area -- with a far larger area than just around Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us at that time period in May who Lieutenant-Colonel Pavle Milinkovic was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavle Milinkovic, Lieutenant-Colonel, was the commander of the 1st Posavina Brigade and before that, while it was still part of the JNA, he was the commander of the 395th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what position Captain Momcilo Petrovic had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, what position Captain Momcilo Petrovic had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momcilo Petrovic was the chief of security at the command staff of the 1st Bosnia Brigade in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know that the Brcko Brigade, the Posavina Brigade, if you'd like to call it that, was small and so you must have known an MP named Pero Rekanovic from the village of Bukvik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Pero Rekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't know all the MPs in the Posavina Brigade where you were Chief of Staff in May?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was there briefly and my job was different. The nature of work within a military department, or a draft board, is very different from the nature of work of a brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I seek clarification? Earlier, you referred to the Posavina Brigade in Brcko. You were then asked whether that was also known informally as the Brcko Brigade. You said, "I don't know how people called it." Now in one of your recent answers you referred to the Brcko Brigade. Is, for you, the Brcko Brigade the same as the 1st Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought that was the case and I've asked the witness. I'll try to stay with the 1st Posavina Brigade, if that's what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. And that is -- let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've testified in the Karadzic trial here, haven't you, recently?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you provided a similar signed statement to the Trial Chamber in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you acknowledge that in that signed statement, you did not mention Brcko in your biography?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you did not mention your time in Brcko during those key spring months of April, May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, it's the position of the Prosecution that the reason you did not mention those is because you were involved in criminal events during that time. Did you know, at the time that you signed your report for the Karadzic case, that you had been named by a witness in the Krajisnik trial as ordering the killing of a Muslim -- excuse me, of a Croat man named Franjo Vugrincic, V-u-g-r-i-n-c-i-c?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before you answer this question, I would like to inform you that if a true answer to that question would tend to incriminate yourself, that you may ask the Court to be relieved from answering that question, because there is a basic rule that you cannot be forced to answer a question, whether that would tend to incriminate you, irrespective of what the Court could do then, that is to say that you should answer the question but under those circumstances, your answer could not be used against you. I would like to inform you about this right. Therefore, do you remember the question that Mr. McCloskey put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. McCloskey put several questions and I will answer, I will certainly answer all of the questions he put to me. First of all, what was the first question, whether I recall the events in May in Brcko? I can't remember what your question was. Can I answer the second question while I recall this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one. First of all, Mr. McCloskey did put to you that the reason that you did not mention your time in Brcko was because you were involved in criminal events during that time. That was the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not true. The exclusive reason why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Now, the second question was whether you were aware that a witness had named you as having ordered the killing of a Croat by the name of Franjo Vugrincic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not order the killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were aware that a witness had named you for ordering that killing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. That was the question. Mr. McCloskey may put further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you failed to mention your Brcko experience to the Karadzic -- in the Karadzic statement, you were aware that a witness had testified at the Krajisnik trial about your ordering the killing of Franjo Vugrincic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer that question? That's a lie, a pure lie. First of all, as the chief of the military department, between the 9th until the 20th of May, I was outside of that area in the Piperci village upon orders of the military command which was a village about 20 kilometres from Brcko. So at the time when this crime was committed, I was not in Brcko at all. Secondly, as far as I know, and also pursuant to a fireman's -- a fire-fighter's statement who said this happened on the 10th of May, at the time I was the chief of the military department and not in the brigade staff, so I had absolutely no competence and no authority over brigade units. At the time the Chief of Staff of the 1st Posavina Brigade was Major Slobodan Milinkovic. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you failed to put in your Brcko experience in your Karadzic statement, in addition to being aware of the Krajisnik witness, were you aware that the Krajisnik Trial Chamber, in paragraph 327, concluded, and I quote, "On 10 May, one of the workers detained at the fire station was shot on the orders of JNA Captain Sehovac." Were you aware of that conclusion by the Trial Chamber in the Krajisnik case of this institution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put two questions to me. First of all, in my statement, I did not mention Brcko because I was instructed not to do so by the Defence counsel of Mr. Karadzic's. He said that we would only deal with Sarajevo. That was the only reason. The second question was I was advised here at the court, I was informed, that there was some kind of statement by some fire-fighter in Brcko at the time, although I wasn't even in Brcko at the time. We had had so much work. We were swamped with work. We worked 10 to 12 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You go back to the event itself on which you have elaborated already. The second question was whether you were aware that the Krajisnik Trial Chamber had concluded that, on the 10th of May, one of the workers detained at the fire station was shot on the orders of JNA Captain Sehovac. Were you aware of such a finding by the Krajisnik Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about that at the Karadzic trial. Until that time, I had not known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The witness at the Krajisnik trial testified that you ordered your soldiers to take the victim out and kill him and the witness also testified that he'd thought you'd ordered the victim to take his shoes off. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a single soldier in my formation in my establishment. I only had civilians. They were men and women, highly educated. The only officer that I had was the security officer. That's one. And secondly I was not present at the fire-fighting department and I ordered no shoes to be taken off. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you -- in May or June 1992, did you become aware of an open mass grave with the bodies of non-Serbs, just on the outskirts of Brcko, on the banks of the Blizna river?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think now we are moving beyond any issues related to the witness and moving into other crimes in Brcko which are out of the scope of the indictment and are therefore not to be part of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this grave is related to the victim that was identified in the Krajisnik case and by the witness as having been ordered to be killed by this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, but it's not a response to what Mr. Ivetic said, that it's outside the scope of the indictment and not part of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This goes to his credibility, that he is involved in criminal events and his -- actually his statements to prior cases I think are shown to be covering that up. So I think it's important that the Trial Chamber know that this comment of the witness, that as you'll see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It goes to credibility. That's your answer. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you hear of this mass grave or see it right near where you were stationed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither saw nor heard of any mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 65 ter 30975?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, in 1996, the Time magazine published this photo and noted in the article that it was in the Brcko area from May and June of 1992, and, sir, I can tell you that if you look in the right-hand corner of this photograph, you'll see a bare foot and leg. That is the -- the investigation has revealed that is the leg of Franjo Vugrincic. Look at that photo, please. Look up now in the left-hand corner. Do you recognise what that is? Is that a truck?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left top corner?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. It looks like a truck, a refrigeration truck, something like that, and I can see a body in front of it and a man standing by the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear about this mass grave when you were there on duty in the Brcko area? And did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about this, and as I've said, I had not heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can go to another subject. In December of 1994, when you were part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I guess you were the commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In December of 1994, were you involved in the shooting death of a Serb man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Serb you are referring to. Could you remind me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you issue orders that resulted in the death of a man named Stojan Ilic -- Elez?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In relation to this case, I should like to say this: I know this happened on the 13th or the 14th of December. I went to the military court because of that. In Bileca, there were complete proceedings conducted on that score and I was acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who is Stojan Elez?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 65 ter 30918? Should be page 10 and 11 in English, page 6 in the B/C/S. Excuse me, let's go now to page 10 in the English. Are we there? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that this is a document from the Republika Srpska office of the military prosecutor, the Army of Republika Srpska, and if we look -- excuse me, if we look briefly through it, we can see that it's dated 5 September 1995 and it's entitled, "Information on Crime Trends for August 1995." And it goes through various crimes and crime trends, political crimes, crimes against the army, other crimes. And now we are on page 10 where it says, "Other Crimes," and if we go to page 11, in the English, and as I said, it should be page 6 in the B/C/S, take some time to read it. You'll see your name there: "On about 1800 hours on 13 December 1994, after members of the so-called army of BiH carried out an attack on the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, on the Gojcina Ravan, on the slopes of Mount Igman, when the unit withdrew to establish a new defence line, Colonel Sehovac ran into a soldier, Sreto Vitkovic, near the check-point near Kijevo, who abandoned his position following the attack and seeking that he was intending to move away, and asked him, Where are you fleeing? And then ordered him to return to the battalion which Vitkovic did not do but headed to a nearby parked Renault 4 car driven by Stojan Elez. He sat in the car that also carried Milica Lalovic and told the driver to start, which he did. Then Colonel Sehovac ordered military policeman Borislav Jevdic and Ignjat Vidakovic to fire at the car which Jevdic did by firing two bullets individually, one of which struck Stojan Elez in the back inflicting an entry wound of which Stojan Elez died. Milica Lalovic, is that a woman or a man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milica is a woman's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is Stojan Elez?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Stojan Elez. He was a driver of this Renault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this a correct accounting of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You ordered two MPs to fire on a man that was getting into a car with a woman and a man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not order that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had no involvement in this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved, but that is not what I ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The MPs did it on their own?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They did that pursuant to my order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did order them to fire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not at people, but to fire in the air, warning fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Like in the movies?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What movies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question. Mr. McCloskey, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use this kind of judgement when you issued orders for your troops to fire on the Muslim forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will go on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to put a question to the witness. Mr. Sehovac, you said, first, when you were asked by Mr. McCloskey, who is Stojan Elez, "I don't know." Later on, you said to the same question, and who is Stojan Elez, "I did not know Stojan Elez. He was a driver of this Renault." Why did you first say, "I don't know"? You knew about this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know him personally. He was not from my unit. This was a person of whose name and surname I heard only at the trial in Bileca, before the military court in Bileca, during the trial that was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you were asked by Mr. McCloskey who is Stojan Elez, you should have answered that. Why didn't you do that? Because you knew his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I gained the impression that he's asking me such questions that I can either answer or I cannot answer or there is somewhere in between. I do not have the impression that he's asking me genuinely about what had happened so that I can genuinely say. Regarding Brcko, for instance, he won't let me explain, explain anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question since you were moving subjects, moving -- changing topic, Mr. McCloskey. Did you report the insubordination by those who did not fire in the air but apparently fired in such a way that casualties were the result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of those of the two soldiers opened fire, the first time in the air. The second time I ordered that they shoot at the tyres of the vehicles. The bullet ricocheted and that is how it hit Stojan Elez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your previous answer was incomplete where you said "I ordered them to fire in the air," whereas the complete answer would have been "I ordered them to fire in the air and after that to fire at the tyres." That would have been the complete answer and the complete truth rather than the partial answer that you gave. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of that. The gentleman did not allow me to say everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not true in this respect. Where Mr. McCloskey cut you short at other moments, he -- let me -- first you were asked whether you ordered to fire on a man that was getting into a car. You said, "I did not order that." You were asked about your involvement. You said, "I was involved but that is not what I ordered." You were then asked whether the MPs did it on their own. You said, "No. They did that pursuant to my order." You were then asked, "So you did order them to fire?" And then you said, "Yes, I did, but not at people, but to fire in the air, warning fire." And there you should have said, "I gave them two orders - the first to fire in the air, the second to shoot at the tyres of the car." That would have been the proper answer, if I understand the rest of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, the follow-up question, "As in the movies?" The witness was answering and Your Honour directed to move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree there. Okay. Let's leave it apart whether -- but you have not answered my last question, that is, did you report the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an on-scene investigation immediately afterwards. I put this soldier Elez in an ambulance and sent him to the hospital in Trnovo. There was a surgical team there, and the team of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps arrived at the scene and conducted an on-site investigation immediately. So that everything was reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While your answer is a bit ambiguous, you said there was an on-scene investigation immediately afterwards. Was that because you had reported the event to the competent authorities for the on-scene investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that was one of the reasons, and the second reason is that it is their obligation because a soldier died --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are evading my question, whether you suppose it was one of the reasons. My question was did you report it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did. I reported it to the Chief of Staff of the corps, who arrived at the scene five minutes after the event, to Colonel Cedo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Cedo Sladoje, Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you report it by -- through what means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orally. We had a meeting at the school in Kijevo because it was the assessment of the command of the brigade that the positions in Gojcina Ravan, and Mocevici had fallen because units had fled from positions. And on that day, the brigade had 18 dead and I do not remember the exact number of wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by your answer. You said we had a meeting at the school in Kijevo. Was that after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to that meeting in Kijevo, because this happened very near the school, a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the meeting in Kijevo was after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Sladoje was already there in that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was not. He ordered me - he was in Trnovo; I was in Mocevici - that we come to Kijevo. Was it 4.00 or 5.00? I don't remember exactly. At the time -- at the very moment I arrived at the school in Kijevo, this incident happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were ordered to go to the school, and when you went to that school, being close to that school, then the event happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly back into this. Colonel, would you agree with me, and you've stated that you were taught about the laws of war, that it is not illegal for a commander to shoot a soldier that is wilfully abandoning his post in combat, and fails -- and disregards an order to stay put?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that. But according to the rules of war of the former JNA, abandoning posts was to be -- was to be prevented at any cost, as was the loss of positions. Even if force had to be used, losing those positions would entail very serious consequences for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and for the entire army of the Republika Srpska too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the question you put to the witness is confusing because the witness said that he ordered to shoot at the tyres, and that the result was caused by a ricochet. Now, in your question, you implicitly, without making this very explicit, you still present the Prosecution's position, ignoring more or less the answer of the witness, that he had ordered to shoot at a soldier. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you remain commander of your brigade after this incident, through the end of your time period when you left for back surgery, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But this trial actually happened very soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this incident did not affect your career at all? You remained in command at all times?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did affect my career. I had to go through this entire process of this trial at the military court in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would like to tender that exhibit, 65 ter 30918. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30918 receives number P6675, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you've acknowledged, and as is normal, you spoke with Defence counsel and added some more information to your statement. We received a note from Defence counsel from contact he had with you on Friday that stated, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. First let's deal with the -- because that's not in evidence at this moment because it was not uploaded into e-court. It was the -- it was MFIed yesterday as D560. I do understand that meanwhile it has been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour, under the 65 ter number - one moment, please - that we originally had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be 1D2834?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, any objection against admission of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D560 is admitted into evidence. So you can now proceed on the basis of what is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe what I'm referring to was not involved -- it was not part of that which is also, I don't think, necessarily abnormal and I'm sure counsel will agree. I'm just reading the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, that's fine. But at least this matter has been dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got an e-mail from my colleague that says, "Further, the witness today" -- and that was Friday -- "recalled specific details about the Butmir tunnel, including its manner of use and capacity. He stated that the VRS did not target the tunnel due to the close proximity of UN personnel near the entrance of the same." Is that correct? Is that roughly what you had told Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom did I say that? I apologise. To Defence counsel? Is that what you're asking me? I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I got an e-mail from Mr. Ivetic on Friday that told me about, as is completely normal, what you had talked to him about, and I just read the part of that e-mail to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the VRS did not target that Butmir tunnel because there was UN personnel near it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the distance between the entrance of the tunnel and the UNPROFOR forces, the UN forces, was only about 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other part of the question was whether, for that reason, you refrained from targeting the Butmir tunnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the reason, Your Honour. We feared there might be casualties on the UN side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you also fear that you might get retaliated on by NATO and bombed if you did that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. I did not fear it. I don't know about the others. But I don't think that would have been the reason for NATO to order air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I notice it's break time and I should be done within the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first. Mr. Sehovac, we will take a break of 20 minutes. Will you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will wait for the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to Exhibit 65 ter 30974, and this is a blowup from our map book, which was Exhibit P3 at page P48. Colonel, this is going to be a blowup of what was I believe a big VRS map. I think Mr. Groome, for Your Honours, I think he actually had the physical map in court the other day. But I've just blown up this particular part of it, and we have drawn on this map one -- well, the ERN number up in the right-hand corner is from the ICTY, but we've also put on this green line to represent the approximate location of the Butmir tunnel. And if you could just study the map briefly, does this map accurately depict where the tunnel was in relation to the front lines as depicted on the map, the red being, as we've learned, the VRS, and the blue being the Muslim BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see a little flag above a -- looks like a town called Grlica. Do you know what that flag depicts? The one on the left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. That is a flag with the number 2 inscribed. That was the command post of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the flag to the right of that, what is that, closer to Vojkovici?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That flag depicts the command post of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. That was my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it that where you spent a good amount of your time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, yes, but later on, we moved the main command post to the sector where the roads intersect. That's about 500 to 600 metres to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this line that we see above the flag for your command post, it's semi-dotted and it has little half circles in it. I was told that that was the border line between your brigade and the 1st Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade; is that correct? 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the right border of my brigade and it shows that my brigade defended the right zone, to the east of Kamenjaca, trig point 665.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last place name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last place name you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village Gornje Mladice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And looking again at your -- where your command post flag is, under the town of Vojkovici, there appears to be something like an X with a sort of a circle in it in red, right on that road. What does that symbol depict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What cross? Do you mean the black colour? Below Vojkovici? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the red colour right below Vojkovici on the main road. It's a red dot and looks like it might have a cross over it, or an X of sorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that in a circle or is a circle in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's actually in a circle now that I look at that part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depicts the position of the brigade fire group, of my brigade, 120-millimetre mortars. However, it is not marked properly here. That's not where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you did have mortar positions in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, but they were 82-millimetre mortars at the beginning of the war, in the valley of the Zeljeznica river. Later on, I repositioned them to Duga Kosa and Papas Brda village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you had received orders in 1995, in May of 1995, to shell the entrance, either entrance of the Butmir tunnel, you could have dropped some mortars on the entrances of the tunnel, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. They were too far, the fire positions. I don't know what the scale is here. Is it 1 to 50.000 or 1 to 100.000? It doesn't show.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of those squares is two kilometres that you see, the grid squares, and you know how long the tunnel -- you've just told us how long the tunnel --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's roughly accurate. So that tunnel is some 800 metres. So you're within a kilometre of that tunnel by this map.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire position, no, no. Absolutely not. It was five to six kilometres away. They were in the sector of Gornje Mladice in 1995. You don't -- I can't see it here. It's Papas Brdo, some six to seven kilometres to the entrance to the tunnel. And here you can see that this was -- the tunnel was even outside my area of responsibility. And I was assigned this area of responsibility only in the later half of August 1993. The right side -- the right-hand border was the Zeljeznica river. Up until now -- up until then I held sector 1 and Dobrinja 4, together with parts of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us what the range of a 120-millimetre mortar is at the maximum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was about six kilometres and some 300 or 400 metres, with the shells that we had. And that was the further-most range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said your firing positions were more than that distance away from the entrance of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can't see it here on this map but that was up on Papas Brdo hill. This is just a section of that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is the maximum range for an 82-millimetre mortar? Same question that the President just asked you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your neighbour, your VRS neighbour, the 1st Brigade, they also had mortars, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30974 receives number P6676, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. If the parties could agree on the -- where the Papas Brdo hill is. I always understood that Brdo means hill, but Papas Brdo, where that is. In order to fully understand the evidence of the witness, we would like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll track that down. We will track it down together, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to Exhibit 65 ter 03511.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a sit-rep dated May 13th, 1995, and drafted by David Harland. And we can see what this is. We see the highlight of it. "Mortar attack kills 10. UNPROFOR considers air strike then decides against it." Let's go to the next page in both languages. And here at the top of the page we see David Harland has written, "Mortar attack on the tunnel, talk about air strikes. Serb gunners bombarded the Butmir entrance to the tunnel that runs under Sarajevo airport on Sunday afternoon, 7 May. There were more than 20 casualties. 11 people were killed. The casualties included both civilians and military personnel. It was the bloodiest violation ever of the NATO ultimatum of 9 February 1994." Sir, is this, in your view, just UN propaganda? Or what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it. It could be the truth. Why would it be propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So given your answers that the VRS never targeted the Butmir tunnel, would you agree with me that you're not a reliable witness on key criminal events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic? One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question is rather vague, speculative and imprecise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're invited to rephrase the question or the questions and perhaps you could be a bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you agree that your testimony that the VRS did not target the Butmir tunnel was flat-out wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything to that effect. These are your words. You just said that. We did target the airport but we did not target the UN forces there. Where can you find that I said that we never fired upon the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to argue with you, but you'll recall standing by the statement that I read to you that I got from Mr. Ivetic where you said, "Further, the witness today recalled specific details about the Butmir tunnel, including its manner of use and capacity. He stated that the VRS did not target the tunnel due to the close proximity of the UN personnel near the entrance to the same." And we can all look back where you agreed that -- and stood by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something for the benefit of the truth here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's an answer to a question, you may. If it is outside the scope of questions, you may not. So, therefore, think about it before you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, it is to do with the question. On the 17th of March and on the 21st of March, we established tactical groups and carry out an attack on Donji Kotorac, with the aim of preventing the crossings across the Butmir airport, which at the time was still being under construction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is too far away from the question. What Mr. McCloskey did put to you, he read to you what Mr. Ivetic had told him in an e-mail which was sent. It was read to you, and Mr. McCloskey asked whether it was correct. And the relevant portion of the e-mail was that he stated that the VRS did not target the tunnel due to the close proximity of UN personnel near the entrance of the same. And you had answered that that was correct. Please proceed. I'll decide on admission. One second, please. There was no objection but no number has been assigned yet. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03511 receives number P6677, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6677 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, prior to my saying no objection to the admission, I believe Mr. McCloskey did, for several lines, say something, so was that a question directed to the witness that the witness is entitled to answer or is Mr. McCloskey making submissions, which is improper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please give me the page and line indications because I moved to another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Temporary transcript page 31, lines 1 through 7. Actually -- yes, 1 through 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was comment, Mr. McCloskey, rather than a question. You apparently argued with the witness rather than to put questions to him on the subject of whether he said -- had said anything about targeting the Butmir tunnel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you want to offer an explanation about the Butmir tunnel targeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I could not reach it with my mortars because they were outside our range. It was -- it had to be done by the 1st Sarajevo Brigade and parts of the corps artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During your time as the commander of the brigade, did you meet with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in some of those occasions, did you meet with the other brigade commanders of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and meet -- and go up to Jahorina and sit with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we had regular reports on combat-readiness. Then we would be issued tasks for the forthcoming period, and we almost -- almost always there would be someone from the Main Staff of the VRS, and frequently it would be General Mladic who would attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during those meetings, did General Mladic inform you of the military objectives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "military objectives"? I don't understand. Would you please clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did General Mladic talk to you about what the plans of the VRS were towards the enemy, and what kind of orders you would be receiving and could expect to receive? Just --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean strategic objectives of the VRS? Yes. General Mladic always had a vision, and whatever was relevant for us, he would always present to us. Of course, I didn't have insight into everything. This was the Supreme Command. And the Main Staff of the VRS, these are the highest levels of command in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And yesterday, at page 24033, lines 9 through 11, you said, "In addition, we carried out numerous active operations such as diversions at the forward end of the enemy and similar." So did your brigade have a diversionary unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We conducted active combat. We engaged in active combat. And that would be from groups of soldiers to company level. A special diversionary group, we did not have, but we had trained men who could carry out a diversionary action. These were officers and they would be primarily from the engineer corps. That would be the military specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these diversionary units, would they go behind enemy lines to conduct their operations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And all armies have them. They would go blow up things and disrupt the enemy in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it is always one of the tactical objectives of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to now go to Exhibit P0358. These are entries of General Mladic's war diaries, and if we could start at -- I believe it should be e-court page 181, and thankfully the language -- the numbers are the same, I see, in both -- both languages. And, sir, it's the position of the Prosecution, and I -- that these are handwritten notes from general -- that General Mladic made at various meetings, and you'll see, as we get there, there is a version in the Serbian that is typewritten that may be easier to read. But do you -- do you recognise General Mladic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't recognise the handwriting of General Mladic. How would I? How could I?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a lot of noise in the microphone possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we adjust the microphone so as not touch the shoulder -- no, no, don't move it away from your voice but, rather, redirect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it may be easier for the witness to go back to the transcribed version, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We see this is dated May 31st, 1993, with some ministers. Let's go to the next page. And we'll see that there is a meeting on 2 June 1993 with representatives of the RS, the authorities with commanders of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and authorities in the zone of the corps. And I don't want to spend a lot of time with this but if -- if you could just look at this, let's slowly go over to the next page, as you've seen, that it's General Galic. In this context, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Stanislav Galic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we go to the next page, 183, we see a Colonel Lizdek. Who's that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vlado Lizdek was the commander of the 1st Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the same page we see Colonel Rado Dzicic, the Ilidza Brigade. Let's go to 184. And we see other people who I'm sure are familiar to you. Let's go to 185. And we see here Lieutenant-Colonel Sehovac, and that's of course you. And we see -- does this -- the notations of "heavy losses, unsuccessful in offensive combat activities, deserters 164, 14 per cent, the largest part joined MUP units, work obligation ..." does that help -- would that have been information you had reported to General Mladic and he would have written down?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my report to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- apparently the microphone of the witness is not switched on. Is it on now again, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was my report to the corps commander. These were soldiers who had left the brigade. Part of them joined the Ministry of the Interior units, part of them were assigned to work obligation, and part of them deserted, fled, for Serbia. There were such individuals who left Republika Srpska to escape the war and fled. So in total, that was 164 men, in other words 14 per cent of the brigade component.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall being in Jahorina and making this report in the presence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, of course. We reported, we submitted reports to the corps commander, to General Mladic. We were open. We always were frank. He knew our -- General Mladic knew our problems and he was very fierce in fighting that. He was against people leaving the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say you submitted reports, you mean orally, to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally, and once the oral report was over, we would hand in a certified written report which would then be sent to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, together with a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe the scene for us? I mean, is it a large room with all these officers in the room?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hotel in Rajska Dolina valley, a military hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were all these officers in one room?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see here number 9, and I don't want to go through all the pages, but if we go on through this, there are various other names, and then we get to people like Tomo Kovac. Who was Tomo Kovac at the time? This was at page 191.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is reference made to Tomo Kovac? In my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. This is in the diary on 191. It will come up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question is who he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was the Deputy Minister of the Interior at that time, if I recall exactly, for a while, but I'm not sure that I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you recall others besides the military being present at this big meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, the presidents of municipalities attended these meetings, the president of the republic would at times also attend the meeting, then the speakers of the assembly, the president of the assembly, the key people who were in charge of the -- of the state and the Army of Republika Srpska. Because we had many common issues to discuss and points in common generally. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go to page 194. Here we see a note that President Karadzic is making a statement. Do you remember President Karadzic being at that meeting making a statement about Sarajevo, as well as other things?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that President Karadzic took the floor. I do not exactly recall -- I cannot recall his exact words because 20 years have elapsed. Were I a computer I would not be able to reproduce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to show you one last exhibit, and that is Exhibit P04517. And I would like -- we've revised the translation because it was a little rough and it also had handwritten portions in it that were hard to make out. So we've asked them to be bolded so that everyone can see clearly the handwritten additions. And if I could give a hard copy to the witness, it may be easier for him to go over it. I've given a hard copy to Mr. Ivetic at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection so, therefore, could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the doc ID for the revised translation is 0649-3781-1 ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you'd like to replace the present English translation with the newly uploaded one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, did you have an opportunity already to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have not. I just found out about this at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that you have another 48 hours to make any comments on the translation, if there is any need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Madam Registrar, you are instructed to replace the present translation in P4517 by the newly uploaded one, doc ID 0649-3781-1 ET. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we are just waiting for, I believe, P04517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is then still the old translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and we really should have the new one. I apologise for -- as it says, "Mr. President," that's actually wrong. It should say "greet all those present," as you'll see from the revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, take a look at the -- at the front page and you'll see that this is from the army of the Republika Srpska Main Staff, dated 31 May 1993. It says, "Submitting conclusions from the assessment of the situation in the SRK zone." And there is no signature or signature block at the end of this. But this document was found at the Mladic residence, in a search that I think everyone is now familiar with. And it's the position of the Prosecution that these handwritten notes were made on this document. We do have the original, if anyone is interested. Now, I just -- I don't want to go over all the details, but it's clearly an assessment of the situation in your corps' zone. We can see that from the front page; isn't that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is right. It refers to the corps. I don't know whether it has anything which pertains to my brigade because I was a commander of the brigade and there I can provide a full and correct answer, because a corps is a huge operational unit which was about 25.000 men strong, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we are going to -- we'll get to that. And we see the handwritten notes up in the corner. It says, "Greet all those present, give recognition to the members of the RSK MUP, the RSK, the MUP, and all levels of authority in the corps zone." I won't read all of it. And I know it's a lot to remember, but is this -- these notes in the right-hand corner, is that the kind of thing Mladic said or would have said at a meeting such as you have described that happened, as we can see, just a couple of days before this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a very nice code of conduct of the Chief of Staff when he addresses high-ranking officers of the corps, commanders of brigades, and representatives of the authorities, and representatives of the Ministry of the Interior. He's always courteous and it is at a very high level. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we go to page 10 briefly in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have seven pages in front of me. I do not have ten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you go to the last page in your -- should be the last page of the --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. Number 7 -- number 8, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see there that there is a handwritten note to the president, and that would have been President Karadzic in this context, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whom it refers to. I haven't read it. If you would be so kind as to translate it for me, I could find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back one page in B/C/S? The handwritten note should be on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The beginning of the handwritten note, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's right -- you have it on the screen and it's in front of you in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you ask me a question? I apologise. I didn't quite understand, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm unable to read this handwriting, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'll read it to you briefly, some of it, in English. "Mr. President, gentlemen, discussions have been recorded which we at the GS VRS will study and examine in the shortest possible time and transform into corresponding plans and orders. I ask all of those present to understand that the tasks and positions voiced here by the president of our assembly, General Djukic, our Prime Minister, and you, Mr. President, are binding for all present and do not bear postponement. Your obligation and ours to transform these tasks, as soon as possible, into concrete plans and orders, both in the army as well as in organs of authority, that be our motivating force for new achievements and even greater results. I personally believe in our forces and our power, and I will allow myself the liberty of [text was missing at that point] complete liberation of the corps' zone which is your task of the utmost priority, maximum unity, and a very disciplined and successful functioning of the authorities, army and of the police. I wish you all this in the name of the GS VRS and my own name, and I am convinced that you shall persevere on these extremely responsible tasks." So who do you think said -- drafted these words on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was drafted obviously by General Mladic. If you will allow me to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a comprehensive analysis in the zone of combat activities of the corps, and the situation with the organs of authority, the highest ranking officer, and that was General Mladic, would always have the final word. After his final concluding remarks, we would soon have specific tasks for specific command levels which would be submitted to the corps command and the corps command would translate those into tasks for commanders of brigades. So this is a -- these are final remarks by the commander, very appropriate, very decent, encouraging also for all of us because it refers to the liberation of the entire zone of the corps and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You go far beyond the scope of the question. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he is noting "president," is that President Karadzic that he is addressing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Possibly in some parts he's referring to the president of the assembly but I suppose that he was referring to President Karadzic as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to page 8 in the English, that's page 5 -- that's your page 5, and you'll see it on the screen as well, and this point will -- this will be a typed part so you'll be able to read it. We see here there is now a chapter of this document called "Main Problems." So if we could now go to the next page, page 9 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, there is one paragraph I want you to take a close look at. It's the one -- it's the bottom of the page for you, on page 6 and it's in the middle of the page in the English and it -- I'll read it: "The activities of sabotage terrorist groups should be used in further operations, as well as ambushes and surprise activities, so that there is constant negative effect on the morale of the Muslim forces and population, that they have a sense of fear and constant insecurity from the activities of our forces."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I am unable to find it. I have it. It is the last paragraph, "The activities of sabotage terrorist groups should be used in further operations as well as ambushes and surprise activities," okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll continue: "Through tactical acts and our propaganda activity, it is necessary to develop in them a feeling that their fate depends on the Army of Republika Srpska. Through the incessant activity and combat actions of all available SRK forces, losses need to be inflicted on the enemy and a feeling of the dependency, fear and insecurity developed in them." In your view, and you have told us of your studies regarding international law, is there any legitimate military justification for the VRS to use their forces to keep, and I quote, "constant and a negative effect on the Muslim ... Muslim population," as you see it written here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say "Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Mr. McCloskey is going to ask a question arising from the document, he should quote the entire submission, not quoting out of context, pulling parts and joining them together, in the manner that the Prosecutor wishes to present their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two issues. First, the witness asks for a specific portion. Perhaps you could read the relevant portion. Second, some selectivity is allowed and can be redressed in re-examination, Mr. Ivetic, but it should not take a form that it twists the meaning of the portion selected by -- of the relevance of the portion selected by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take a look at the first three lines of the paragraph that you've identified. They say, and I'll read the full ones this time: "The activities of the sabotage terrorist groups should be used in further operations as well as ambushes and surprise activities so there is a constant negative effect on the morale of the Muslim forces and population, that they have a sense of fear and constant insecurity from the activities of our forces." Now, sir, I grant you it's the Prosecution's position that there is no problem using psychological warfare on the Muslim forces, so I'm not asking you about that part of the sentence. The part of the sentence I'm asking you about is when they say that there is a "constant negative effect on the morale of the Muslim forces and population." Is there any legitimate military justification for the VRS to target the population as stated in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not actually the gist of this. It says that the activities of sabotage terrorist groups should be used in further operations as well as ambushes and surprise activities. These are -- so that there is constant negative effects, because all of the actors are affected in a negative way, both the army of the -- the Muslim army, the Bosnian army, and the population. This is the way I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try one more time. Is there any legitimate military justification to target the Muslim population for this kind of activity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, these are the negative effects which are the consequences of legitimate combat actions. I don't know that the Main Staff had any Special Forces for psychological warfare, especially not the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The brigade certainly did not have any such forces. Please ask me questions which pertain to my level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
