utterances.text: -- the language is such that you could understand the use of further operations, ambushes, surprise activities, so that there is, that means or at least it could be understood as the sought effect to be a negative effect not only on the morale of forces but also negative effect to be sought on the population. What Mr. McCloskey asked you is whether you, under international law, whether you're allowed to use military operations in such a way, and with the aim of seeking a negative effect, not only on the forces but also on the population. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sir, I believe that the fate of the population on both the Muslim and the Serbian sides was associated with the fate of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that you are not answering my question. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions. Mr. Ivetic, we are close to the point where we would take a break. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think only about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Then we'll do that after the break. Witness, we'll continue after a break of 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to first touch on the issue that was being discussed just prior to the break, and I'd like to ask you the following question: Based on your training in the JNA, is it permitted under international law to undertake legitimate sabotage and diversionary tactics against enemy armed forces even if those actions lead to negative morale also among the civilian population that is in enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is permitted, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, continue.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this, we cannot see -- I mean, it would not be allowed if some Special Forces, the forces of the VRS or the Main Staff, conducted psychological and propaganda warfare against the population, if they terrorised the population, they instilled fear in them, if they threatened with religious or national ethnic hatred, if they threatened to move them out. Simply, what it -- the position that is stated here simply states the actions that can be undertaken by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear or understand the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last portion of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this text, we cannot see anywhere that the organs of the Main Staff, special organs of the Main Staff of the VRS, are asked to carry out propaganda and psychological activities against the population, meaning to instill fear in the population, to terrorise them, to threaten them with racial or religious hatred and so on. All of this fear, in fact, is the result of the actions by the VRS who have used legitimate means. Here, it mentions diversionary and sabotage actions. Those are quite legitimate. I don't know how else to describe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, have you any further follow-up questions on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On this topic, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there is nothing to be found in this text. The text reads, and I'll read it in English, "so that there is," which could be understood as a result which is specifically sought. Any comment on that? And if there is any translation issue, I'd like to hear, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only shown the last paragraph, and there it says, verbatim, that the diversionary actions should -- and sabotage actions should maintain a level of negative effects on the population, and I don't see that there is anything in dispute there. This is the result of our forces' operations. And it says further on, "By tactical moves and our propaganda activity we should develop in the population the sense that their fate depends on the Army of Republika Srpska," and then it goes on to further talk about the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did put what I consider to be the possibly relevant portion to you. I did it now twice. I do understand how you interpret this text. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, following these meetings in May of 1993, do you recall what military operation was undertaken by the VRS with the involvement of the SRK which arose out of these discussions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Lukavac 93 was carried out which was of operative and strategic significance for the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another topic that the Prosecutor covered with you, Brcko. And I'd like to ask you, during your tenure at Brcko, was the JNA the only armed formation in town or were there other armed formations or paramilitaries in that town?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you -- do you mean the first part of the war? Yes. Using a void or a lacuna that existed from May to June, paramilitary forces used that blank space, as it were, and in June there were the following paramilitary forces: The Red Berets, about 20 of them; Arkan's men, about 30 men; a group from Bor; and a group of Captain Dragan's, whereas in later operations, the so-called Krajina militia, or Milicija Krajine, came and they all came there with one objective only, which was plunder, and we opposed those groups. The president, Mr. Karadzic, and General Mladic sent a unit, I believe, on the 19th of July, under the control of -- under the command of Dragan Andan. It was a unit of the Special Police. We reinforced or strengthened up the -- this unit with members of our military police, developed a plan of combat activities and operations, and we cleansed Brcko and expelled all of these paramilitary units, not only from Brcko but also from a wider territory. I don't know if there is anything more specific that you would like me to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, sir, did you have any personal encounters with any of these paramilitaries in Brcko, and if so, could you please describe these encounters? You personally, individually.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. At this time, in other words from the 23rd of May up until mid-July, in addition to my duties as the chief of the military department, I was also standing in as acting chief of the Posavina Brigade. They actually raided the police station in Brcko, always with the following objective: to steal IDs, passports, drivers' licences and vehicle registration papers, and they would use them when -- to access barracks and other military installations. Until we introduced the curfew, between 8.00 p.m. and 5.00 a.m., and we also set up check-points at all the major intersections in the city, all public buildings in the municipality, hospitals, public enterprises and so on, we forbade anyone from accessing those facilities, or if they were to access them, they shouldn't wear any weapons. Then we also guarded, those we set up guard -- guarding units for those facilities. We also put stickers on vehicles so to prevent their theft. Then we also introduced controls. We controlled the functioning of the entire system of security in the Brcko town, thereby eliminating all paramilitary forces and creating such an atmosphere in the town where civilian authorities and military authorities could function normally. That was our job, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 65 ter number 30959 from the Prosecution's list, and I think it will be on the first page in the B/C/S and the bottom of the first page going on to the second page in the English, item number 3. And, sir, if you could read along with me, it says here: "In Brcko area, forces of the 'Red Berets' have captured the BR, Brcko Brigade, NS, Chief of Staff, Major Milorad Sehovac, the president of the SO Municipal Assembly Brcko and some members of IS, Executive Council, of SO Brcko," and then, if you go to the next page, "put forward the demanded that two members of the Red Berets be released recently arrested by the SRBiH MUP, Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for criminal offences. We have taken stepped up security measures in units and commands, a special unit of SRBiH MUP continues to work on the case." Sir, what can you tell us about this incident where you were apparently captured by this paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a regular combat report from the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps signed by the corps commander Dragutin Ilic, and this is correct. It is true that the president of the municipality and I were arrested because we opposed these forces. And had this special unit not been sent and arrived there, we would have probably been killed. I was released late that evening, around 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would tender the document into evidence at this time as the next Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30959 receives number D562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D562 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on your time period at the Brcko military department. You'd started to give some information during the cross-examination and you were stopped. Could you please describe for us what duties or tasks were undertaken by yourself while at the Brcko military department? What was your role?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a time-frame? That's a -- he was there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe his role remained constant throughout that whole time. If I'm incorrect, the witness can correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness is not there to correct you, but if you say during the whole period of his tenure there, then it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's say in the beginning of the war. Is that specific enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military department of Brcko is a military and territorial institution and it covered the territory of eight municipalities, those of Brcko, Bosanski Samac, Gradacac, Srebrenik, Orasje, Bijeljina, Lopari, Ugljevik and Ugljevik. In this territory, we recruited for the needs of the military forces at the time and for work obligations and military police, about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of privates and officers. The basic tasks of the military department were to keep records, military records, recruitment records, in other words determining the military specialty, then assignment to the JNA, the assignments to military units of the armed forces and also work obligation units, until the deregistration from military records. At the beginning of the war, the military department, or should I -- let me just say how it was organised. In each of the municipalities we had one desk officer. In some cases there were men; in others there were women. In the military department, I was the chief. There was an Albanian, Idris Sajdiju [phoen]. He was my assistant for intelligence. He would just do the screening of the candidates, the recruits, and the other persons were civilians, two who were in charge of recruitment, two for mobilisation. There was a lawyer and also a typist who also kept the logbook. In the beginning we only dealt with recruitment for the needs of the armed forces, and in view of the fact that the Army of Republika Srpska reorganised very soon, the war began in May, and already on the 2nd of June, we -- no, the 5th of July, my apologies, we assigned -- we sent the first group of recruits for military training. The second group was sent in early September. At that time, I was already in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the place.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the military departments were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Various parts of your testimony will be lost if you speak at this speed. You said, "At that time I was already in --" and could you tell us where you were because the interpreters did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning of the war, the Defence counsel asked me, so in the month of May and June, that's when I'm talking about, that period, the early period of the war, we were mostly involved in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You said the following: You were talking about the first group of recruits for military training that were assigned, and then you said the second group was sent in early September. "At that time I was already in --" and then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Vojkovici, or Sarajevo. I was the commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. But I would just like to stress that after I left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do it slowly, then we will not miss anything. Okay. So you said I would just -- you would just like to stress that after you left -- what did you want to stress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to stress that the military department, there was always continuity in the work of the military department. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've identified one soldier and several civilians that worked in the military department with you. Were the civilians armed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned there were just two officers, me and a lieutenant, an Albanian by ethnicity. And I would also like to mention here before the Trial Chamber that the military department was multi-ethnic, so there were Serbs, Albanians, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't part of the question. So just focus on the question that's asked. If there are relevant other matters to be reviewed, then the parties will ask you for it. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have command over any combat units apart from these civilians and one officer while at the Brcko military department?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat: The civilians were not armed. I did not have any competence over, nor could I command, any operative complements, either JNA or Territorial Defence or the newly established VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the office was multi-ethnic. What ethnicities of persons were being subjected to the summons or call-up for military service that were issued by your office?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone received call-ups, calls up. Serbs, Muslims, the Gorani, depending on which unit was being mobilised and where those people lived. Well, that's -- that's it. I'm trying to be focused, as the Judge told me I should be. So everyone received calls up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you heard during cross-examination that a witness identified a Captain Sehovac as having been involved in the killing of a Croat man with the last name Vugrincic. Sir, can you confirm for us what rank you held while you were at Brcko in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, today, the Prosecutor asked you about meetings you attended where General Mladic was present along with presidents of the municipalities, the president of the republic, and MUP representatives. At any of those meetings, did anyone ever discuss any plans for the VRS to target and attack the civilian population in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I state this very explicitly, not at a single meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my last question, sir: At any of these meetings that you attended where General Mladic was present, did he ever issue any orders that you, as an officer, viewed as either criminal or illegal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received an order of that nature from General Mladic throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. On behalf of my client and the rest of the team, I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that completes the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. McCloskey, I would have one question for you. You told us that paramilitary forces used a lacuna, you also called it "that blank space," as it were, and you referred to several paramilitary forces, among them Arkan's men. Do you have any knowledge as to what triggered Arkan or Arkan's men to enter that region? And you were specifically, I think, talking about Bijeljina. Any idea on how they came to be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arkan's men came to Brcko exclusively in order to loot and plunder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they came on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, without any invitation from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that be true for Brcko only or would that have been for the whole region, which is the northeastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the entire region, but I know about Brcko because I lived and worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, any questions? Further cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have a map which I think the witness could probably very simply mark, this Papas Brdo. It's also -- it should be electronically here momentarily if you want to just resolve that. It's a big hill. I don't know where the positions were located according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We earlier looked. Is that a larger map than the one we saw on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it includes the area of Papas Brdo now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't no objection to this being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it uploaded already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's happening as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better to have the marking done electronically so that we have a consistent set of exhibits. I know these are large documents, I'm aware of it. If you'll bear with us for a moment, Witness, you'll be shown a map soon and you'll be invited to mark it. That is the same grid on that map, Mr. McCloskey? Two kilometre squares?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it takes a while for it to be electronically prepared. Mr. McCloskey, although the Chamber has full confidence in the accuracy and the speed your case manager develops, I do understand from her body language that it's almost up, and is confirmed by the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, 65 ter 30978. And can we blow it up one more shot? It might make it a little clearer. Okay. I think that covers it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this does not have the tunnel in it. This is the raw map. And, sir, if you could just study it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness assist so that the witness could mark? Yes, I'm sorry, the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should I mark? The positions of the mortars? The mortar battery and the mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there was Papas Brdo. Could you please mark that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Papas Brdo. I shall first mark Papas Brdo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could be asked to speak into the microphone. We can hardly hear him, or not at all in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I've marked Papas Brdo. The firing position of the mortars were -- the firing positions of the mortars were here, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where the witness marked what seems to be an horizontal oval, he marked a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, under the letter K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second, witness. Where the witness marked with more or less an horizontal oval, he marked Papas Brdo, which is found, as the text under his markings as well. And then just above that, he indicated where the mortar positions were, to the left of the letter K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the distance from those positions to the tunnel, if the grid square is two kilometres, is considerably less than six kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is six -- about six kilometres, but the tunnel is not my zone of operations. That is the zone of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. I should like to stress that. But we can measure it. It is over six kilometres. If this is correct, we can take a ruler and measure it to a T, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that. We'll do that. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think we can offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document as marked by the witness receives number P6678, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I leave it to the parties whether they want the Chamber to measure the approximate distance or whether the parties could agree on it. It shouldn't make that much of a difference. This concludes your testimony, Mr. Sehovac. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Defence, and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, the Chamber was informed that you would like to raise a preliminary issue before the next witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see Mr. Ivetic, however standing. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Associated exhibits. I don't know if you want to deal with that now. We had deferred until the end of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can deal with it, and then I take it Mr. McCloskey will stay with us for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was planning on requesting to be excused, but I, of course, would always stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Associated exhibits in relation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With this witness of course, I don't think there was any problem of course. I forgot about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the number even is any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have cut it down to 12, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cut it down to 12. Although its more exceptionally we allow for a few more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could place on the record, there is one that is a duplicate. 65 ter number 11913, which is at paragraph 66 of the statement, is the same as 1D02187, which is at paragraph 68 of the statement. So we would only tender the 1D02187 in lieu of tendering two times the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something makes me think that I recently saw a short comment that although they look very much the same, that there is slight difference in, I think, some handwriting on it or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If that's the case, then I have no problem with both coming in. I just wanted to try to be as economical as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a look at it. There are no objections. Madam Registrar, could you please prepare a list with numbers and reserve already, I think, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, 13 if we are going to do both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the range of numbers would be D563 up to and including D575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we tender them both, Mr. Ivetic, perhaps you can have a look at it, and for the time being we reserve 12 numbers. I do understand that it was 11913, which would be the duplicate of 1D02187, 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade document, implementing an SRK command order for placing units at combat-readiness, which is described in the other report strictly confidential number 1684-1, dated the 14th of August 1994, signed by Sehovac, Milorad. That seems to be the two documents which may have an overlap. Let's, for the time being, reserve 12 numbers and leave out 11913. And if there is any need at a later stage to have them both, then we'll hear from you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Therefore, 12 numbers would be D563 up to including D574, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D563 up to and including D574 are admitted into evidence. Mr. McCloskey, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. President, I would support a simple measurement of the map as you suggested by the Trial Chamber. I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to take a few moments to talk about a disclosure issue in the agreement of the parties. As the Chamber is aware, the parties reached an agreement to resolve the issues created when the Defence failed to meet the discovery deadline of 5 May 2014. Among the provisions of the agreement was that the Defence would disclose statements of the remaining witnesses as soon as practical and no later than 15 August 2014. As a practical note, we have received no statements from the Defence regarding witnesses in the case other than those for which 92 teres have been filed. The Defence advised us that they would call the next witness, Dragan Milanovic, viva voce. He has never testified. We do have a 65 ter summary for him, but there has been no discovery of a statement or interview notes or anything of that nature. At 7.14 last night, we received an e-mail that reads: "The previous draft statement for Mr. Milanovic has apparently been signed in the interim, though we have now agreed to go viva voce with him. The same is uploaded in e-court as 1D01659 and is hereby disclosed to you in accordance with Rule 67. The Defence will not be tendering this statement." A review of the 11-paragraph statement reveals that there were three interviews with this witness and that it was signed on the 7th of June 2014. Now, with respect to this witness, this is a disclosure violation but it should not preclude cross-examination. There were some additional facts in the statement but we believe we'll have the ability to use our techniques and investigate those issues for cross-examination. However, the overall concern here is that we are increasingly concerned about the status of the Defence discovery and whether they are going to make the 15 August 2014 deadline. We are a month away from that deadline at this point. So at this point, given some of the issues that have come up with respect to discovery, the Prosecution would simply suggest that this may be a time where it would be appropriate for the Chamber to request a detailed report from the Defence as to the status of their statement gathering and disclosure and perhaps have weekly reports from the Defence until the discovery process is completed. And that's it, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. We will consider your request. Any explanation as to why a statement which I do understand was signed on -- was it the 7th of June? Yes. Was not disclosed any earlier than mid-July?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All I can say is I can check with my case manager and maybe inform you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it's your responsibility. I mean the 7th of June, it's not a day or a week, but it's well over a month, which should have been noted already. I'll give you an opportunity to consult with your case manager, but it will not come as a surprise to you that it will take something to explain that. Let's proceed for the time being. And could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, also, Mr. Lukic, having looked at the 65 ter statement, I would strongly advise you and invite you to deal and certainly deal primarily with matters which are of core relevance to this case, and not with marginal issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milanovic. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Milanovic. Mr. Milanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Milanovic -- good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us for the record your first name and your last name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Dragan Milanovic from Foca, the son of Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of April 1961 in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you live after you were born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished my primary and secondary school in Foca. Then I studied in Sarajevo for six years and then I returned to Foca where I continued to reside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What duties did you perform prior to the very outset of the war in the territory of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in my territory, the settlement of Cerezluk, I was the commander of a self-formed platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many men did you have in your platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: The platoon was about 30 men strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within which formation was this platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: First, the platoon was self-formed, and later it was assigned to a company which was within the framework of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1st Battalion of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Battalion of the Foca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So prior to the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: The platoon existed as a self-formed platoon before the beginning of the conflict, for the protection of the people in the area. There still was no command set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you mean by "self-formed platoon"? How does that come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. In our people, there is a story handed down from generation to generation about crimes done to the Serbian people. Also, in that period, prior to the very outbreak of the war, there exist -- many ugly things had happened between the Muslims and the Serbs of the city and municipality of Foca. So that we, but not only we, because this was done by the Muslims also, believe me, in settlements which were predominantly inhabited by Serbs, drawing the lesson from the previous experiences, in order to protect our property and our kin, next of kin, we posted guards. So we set up this unit from people from the area and we posted guards. I was chosen to be their commander. So we posted guards in order to avoid any situations befalling us where we might come to harm, as we had in the Second World War. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the city of Foca proper, before the outbreak of the conflicts, how were the people organised in mixed communities, in mixed settlements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was about to say. Foca is a specific city, a specific town, where the population was greatly mixed. There were settlements where the majority of people were Muslims or Serbs. But in the buildings where a neighbour and next to another neighbour and house next to house, with mixed communities, people organised themselves in different ways. First, where they were neighbours, they had joint patrols, they established mixed patrols, in order to avoid conflicts. And in those settlements where the majority was either Serb or Muslim, they set up these mono-ethnic patrols or guards for protection purposes because one could feel in the air that something was about to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the interethnic relations started to deteriorate in the territory of your municipality, what was the direct cause?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, long before that, there was the Focatrans affair, scandal. This was a transport company where the staff were Muslims and Serbs who lived in Foca, and it so happened that pursuant to a management decision, all Serbs from that company were fired. Then the Serbs tried to find a solution, so they rallied, they set up meetings and rallies, and the population from -- the Serbs from Foca organised in that way. But at the time when these protests were announced, when they were supposed to be held, these rallies, the Special Police of the BH republic arrived and they quashed these rallies, but it was done almost by force. And from that moment on, the Serb and Muslim population began to diverge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that you organised in your settlement, Cerezluk, that you organised patrols, village patrols or guards. When did you do this? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: We organised the patrols in late March, around the 28th or 29th of March, in other words about 10 days before the conflict broke out between the Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the Muslims, too, organised similar patrols. When did they organise their own patrols in these predominantly Muslim settlements or purely Muslim settlements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, they, too, had their own patrols in these villages, in their villages. Perhaps that began at about the same time, perhaps a day or two earlier or later. They even set up barricades or check-points, and checked passers-by regardless of their ethnicity. Although more often than not, they would check the people of Serb ethnicity who would pass in that area, who would pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know about these barricades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I moved around the town a lot, because that was part of my job. Well, I had worked that had to do with -- where -- I had to move around town. I actually had a winery or cellar, and I transported the wines and drinks around the town, and that's how I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour. I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when I earlier said that the Chamber would very much like you to focus on what seems to be the core of this case, and looking at the indictment, we are talking about killings in Foca, detention in Foca, et cetera, rather than matters like who was the first or the second to organise patrols, et cetera. I mean, that seems to be -- I'm not saying it's without any relevance, although it's something that we've heard in the various forms in the various municipalities and there seems to be a pattern on which I would not be surprised, also looking at how witnesses are cross-examined on this matter, that is hardly ever, by the Prosecution, that you could agree on that and then to focus and what is at the core of the charge, that is crimes committed for this witness, for example, crimes committed in Foca. I leave it to that for the time being. We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you are still interested, I can try to explain why we were late with disclosure of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can do that in one minute and a half. Otherwise, we will wait until the end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The statement was signed on the 7th of June 2014, as you said, but we received it here on the 17th of June, and then it was sent for the translation. And then when we discussed the last week whom to have here to testify, since some witnesses could not testify because of the objection made by the Prosecution, we switched this witness, since we didn't have time to introduce his statement, we switched him to testify viva voce and immediately, when we decided last week, we released that statement on the 9th of July 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it was a number of reasons. The first that you could have saved is it shouldn't take 10 days for a statement to -- and I don't know whether it was not yet before the 7th of June, when the witness signed it, because you could submit already a statement although at that moment unsigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we planned to have this witness 92 ter, so we thought we had time. But then we asked him kindly if he can jump into some empty space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milanovic, what kind of weapons did you have at the outset, when you organised these patrols?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we each had some side arms. I myself, I had a 7.62 pistol, and I had a licence for it. Some people in the platoon had hunting weapons; some had pistols. We did not all -- all of us, we didn't have, not every person had a weapon but we had some weapons and then we would take turns for whoever was on patrol would carry the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was with the weapons on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the Muslims, at this point in time, when I was stopped at the -- by the patrol, they too had personal weapons. I could see that for myself. But I can say from my own experience, when I was wounded, that I was wounded by a round from an automatic weapon. I also know that they had some Thompson rifles which is a semi-automatic weapon, and they also had automatic weapons because I myself was wounded by a round from an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to your wounding later. We are still discussing the time leading up to the conflict. Now, was there any propaganda spread by the Muslims, and if so, what did it entail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was a journalist in Foca by the name of Semso Tucakovic, and before the conflict broke out, he fled Foca. And then, on Radio Sarajevo, he reported as a correspondent, as it were, from threatened areas. He reported in a very urgent manner about the arrival of 5.000 Arkan men in Foca and such like, so that this of course instilled fear in his own people, in the Muslims, as to what was about to happen, what would follow next and so on. Of course, none of it happened. Nothing like that was in fact the case. And so what happened was that the Muslims began leaving Foca even before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs leave Foca? Did they begin leaving Foca too, before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were Serbian families too, with small children, who had relatives in Serbia or Montenegro. Those people, aware that something was brewing, they began leaving too, but in far smaller numbers than the Muslim families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to where these Muslims who were leaving Foca went? What direction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as for where they went, as far as I know, first, they went to Gorazde, then to Sarajevo. A part of them were going towards Sandzak or Montenegro, depending on where they had families or friends, so they could take shelter. But as you know what the situation was in the former Yugoslavia, everyone had members of family all over the place in various parts, in Serbia, Montenegro and so on. So they left to wherever they could find shelter with their friends or family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I would like to ask you a little bit about the Crisis Staff in your municipality. Do you know approximately when the Crisis Staff was established in the Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: In early April, as far as I can recall, in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, the delegates of Serb ethnicity walked out and declared a -- their own assembly, Assembly of the Serbian People, and I think that at this same time, approximately, in early April, a decision was made by the Serbian people, or rather by their Serbian representatives in the then-Republika Srpska already, that Crisis Staffs should be established in various towns and places. And such a Crisis Staff was established in Foca as well, whose president was Mr. Miro Stanic and its members were prominent people from Foca, for the most part people who were SDS supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the competence of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as it became obvious that the division was inevitable, the Crisis Staff, as far as the Serbian people is concerned, was overall. They had every competency. Later on, the Serbian Territorial Defence took control of the town, and then the Crisis Staff governed or ran all kinds of activities that had to do with whatever was going on in the city, with the life in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now please pull up 1D3525 in e-court. While we are waiting for it to come up, let me ask you this: Do you have any information as to what the competence of the Crisis Staff was vis-à-vis that of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the Crisis Staff is concerned, they were the ones who made decisions and the territorial staff had to implement them, but the TO, the Territorial Defence, had competence over the military police that was established at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document where we see that it says, "The Serbian Municipality of Foca Crisis Staff and the Serbian Municipality of Foca TO Staff." And this is an order to the military police unit. You've already mentioned that Miroslav Stanic was at the head of the Crisis Staff. The other person whose name appears here, was he in fact what it states here, Cedo Zelovic? Do you know whether he was the Staff Commander, the TO Staff Commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Cedo Zelovic was a TO Staff Commander even before the war, so that, yes, this is -- this does correspond to what he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see the name of the Crisis Staff commander on the B/C/S is not the same as the name on the English. Is there any reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only in B/C/S it's usually to -- it's usual to put last name first and first name last, so that's the difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our society, last name is more important, family name, than your own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, we see that here, in cooperation with the public security station, they are supposed to set up traffic controls. Were you a TO member after this period, in other words after the conflict broke out, when your platoon actually joined another formation or became part of another formation, and when you ceased to exist as an independent unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the Crisis Staff issued certain orders, such as this one, or orders of another nature, all these self-organised platoons or smaller units were integrated in the Territorial Defence of the Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, too, receive orders from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3525 receives number D575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Registrar, the last numbers went up to 575.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was corrected because we decided to reserve 12 instead of 13 numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Now I would like to see briefly in e-court, 1D4510.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is just by way of illustration, this document, to show what the powers of the Crisis Staff were, as we discussed earlier. Here we can see that it was agreed by members of the Muslim village of Trosanj and members of the civilian authorities of the Serbian Municipality of Foca and as the third party, the military authorities. In the signature block at the bottom of the page, we see - and we will need the next page in English for this - we see that there are three signatures that appear there. We have on the left-hand side, Muslim representatives from the Trosanj village, on the right-hand side we have civilian representatives, and in the middle at the bottom, the commander of the Crisis Staff, which is obviously the third party that is mentioned in the heading. Did you get orders from the Crisis Staff for taking positions or for searching the terrain or for disarmament?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: All the orders were issued to units at that time. All the Crisis Staff orders were issued to units, either orally or in writing, and you can see from this document that there were some negotiations. I remember that there were some negotiations and that some kind of a document or of a cease-fire was signed, namely the surrender of weapons by people, by Muslims in the village of Trosanj who had weapons, and were protecting their own population in the village of Trosanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tend this document as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4510 receives number D576, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have one or two questions on this document. Mr. Milanovic, am I to understand that Muslims were not members of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that particular point in time, in Foca, they were not members of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What ethnicity composed the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally of Serb ethnicity because we are talking about the 24th of April, the conflicts had ceased long ago in the city. Only in the villages these people remained in their estates, and they had weapons to protect and were protecting their holdings and their families. So from the aspect of the civilian authorities or the Crisis Staff, as still the military authority, they embarked on negotiations for them to surrender their weapons and to continue to live normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they were going to live normally after surrendering both legal and illegal weapons, whereas the Serbs were keeping their weapons if they were members of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't put it that way. The Serb, as you called them, military forces were on the front lines. That was within the territory of Foca municipality, for which the then-civilian authorities comprised of Serbs were competent. They were in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milanovic, was there at a certain point a division among the police in Foca? Was the police divided?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have already talked about this time prior to the very outbreak of the conflicts, and the time between the 6th and 8th of April, there was a division into Muslim police. Actually, the Muslim police left that public security station, and on the other hand there were the Serb police who also at that time had left the police station, but at a later time the Serbs returned to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff issue some proclamations at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, from the establishment of the Crisis Staff, proclamations were issued on a peaceful life in the city, namely calling for a peaceful life to be continued and for no conflicts to be provoked by either side. And all this lasted approximately up to the 8th of April when a part of the city was -- with a predominantly Serb population was shelled for the first time from the launching pad, from a hill above the city.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not catch the name of the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sukovac hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What parts of the city, while we are on the subject, were shelled from Sukovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: They primarily shelled Cerezluk, the part of the city which I referred to initially where I lived, and also a part of the city under the Celovina hill, which also was predominantly inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, at the time of the shelling, were there any Muslims in your section of the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that immediately prior to the outbreak of the conflict Muslims started leaving the city. In the Cerezluk part of the city, as far as I know, there were no Muslim families in these elevated parts which were shelled, which can be associated with the fact that they actually knew that the Muslim forces would attack those sections. So if there had been any inhabitants in those sections, they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek clarification, you earlier testified that the Crisis Staff was established in early April, if I understood the question well. Now, when asked about the proclamations, you said, "Throughout that period, from the establishment of the Crisis Staff, proclamations were issued on a peaceful life," and you ended that sentence by saying that all this lasted approximately up to the 8th of April, and then you described the shelling. Now, "throughout that period" could therefore have been certainly not more than a couple of days. Because if the Crisis Staff is established early April and proclamations were made until the 8th of April, there is not much time left. Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, you see, throughout this time, during the crisis situation, prior to the outbreak of the conflicts, there were talks between the Crisis Staffs -- Staff comprised of Serbs and the Muslims, which I would call also Crisis Staff, which was comprised of reputable Muslims from Foca. And the objective was, the subject of the talk was that there should be peace established throughout the city, and it was for those reasons and in that connection that the Crisis Staff -- Serb Crisis Staff issued these proclamations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's a real answer to my question is a different matter but please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you specify, this is a confusing term perhaps also, when it is translated all this time throughout this period, can you tell us, specifically, how many, for how many days were such proclamations issued - two days, three days, at most eight days? If you're talking from the beginning of April to the 8th of April, can you tell me how many days were in question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I want to say is whether it's a translation issue throughout the period is another matter, but we are talking not about a period of any length but just about a couple of days up to eight days, and that is sufficient for me, unless you have any specific purpose with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just wanted to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the first conflicts, namely after the 8th of April 1992, did the Muslims, i.e. their forces, hold sections of the city of Foca proper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already stated that Foca is a specific city. Apart from the population that was mixed, as I already explained, there were sections of the city predominantly inhabited by Muslims. This is the section of the city which is called Donje Polje and they were holding that section of town under their control up to the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, so during those four or five days from the 8th to the 12th, were there any private prisons in Muslim territory where Serb civilians were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they did detain -- they did imprison Serb civilians in that area, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After these four days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They held prisoners in that period to the best of the knowledge of the witness. That doesn't assist the Chamber. First of all, the relevance, I don't know whether it's tu quoque or whether it's anything else or it's just background, but then we would like to know how many were detained so that we have facts rather than sweeping statements. Sweeping statements do not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milanovic, you heard I was warned by the Chamber that these sweeping statements are of no assistance to the Chamber so I shall ask you: Do you know personally in what places Serbs were imprisoned? Do you know how many Serbs, who held them? Do you have any concrete knowledge along those lines? And if not, we shall then go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: If it would suffice for the Chamber, there was the penitentiary Foca there in that section and that was their prison where they held detainees. I don't know the exact number. And it did not last long because full control of the city of -- of the city was assumed by Serb territorials on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, the penitentiary, was that -- could you tell us where that was, what location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The penitentiary is on the way to the hospital, on the other side opposite the old bridge on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is that the place where later non-Serbs were held in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, those Serbs that were detained there for a number of -- limited number of days, were they captured during those days or were they imprisoned there already before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were already in prison, and there were men and women and children whom they put in prison there on the pretext of actually protecting them from the shells or from the shooting that came from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What days -- when did this exactly happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the period from approximately the 7th or 8th to the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us names, especially of women and children, that were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I could not give you any specific names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know the -- do you know of any of them from personal knowledge or is it what you heard or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was -- this was told by Serbs who were in Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any name of any male Serbs detained there, arrested and detained there, between the 7th and the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not give you any specific names because in that period, I was on the front line, so we were holding the lines towards the village of Zugovici and I was not in the city. But I heard in later talks that the Serbs, women and children and men, were detained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have -- you have overconcentrated on the cursor that I warned you about. You don't have to focus on it that intently. You don't have to follow its movement that intently. So after the four days of combat, what happened with Muslim combatants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: After these four days, Muslim combatants withdrew from the sections of the city that they were holding towards Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the Muslim population in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim population which remained in Foca continued to live normally as far as it was possible for both the Muslim and the Serb population in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any humanitarian relief campaigns, drives, organised, assistance, to aid to the population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, after the outbreak of conflicts, and that is probably the case in all wars and in all similar events, the first thing that happens is for food stores -- food stores get looted, and in this part of the city where I live, we organised a store house where we actually brought all the food from the shops. And these were mainly shops owned by state companies, and we distributed that food to all the inhabitants in that particular section, including the Muslims who remained in that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please switch his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Thank you. That concludes our working day and I believe that we shall have to continue in the morning tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic, we will adjourn for the day and we will continue tomorrow. We would like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning, but I first want to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever it may be about your testimony, whether that's testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is clear, Your Honour.
